To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NIR optical imaging can be used for the non-invasive and longitudinal study of the biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of nucleic acid-based therapeutics.
NIR optical imaging can be used to monitor the in vivo distribution and fate of nanocarriers and to follow the expression and silencing of reporter genes.

the use of NIR fluorophores and imaging methods allows for the detection of nucleic acid delivery in vivo, and for the monitoring of the resulting biological effect, such as gene expression, in a noninvasive manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new nanocarriers based on DNA and siRNA for gene therapy.
the development and optimization of NIR optical imaging methods to monitor the in vivo distribution and fate of nanocarriers.
the development of NIR fluorophores for the imaging of nucleic acids in living subjects and with the use of NIR fluorophore labeling to study the fate of nucleic acid carriers in mice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
optical imaging is a powerful tool to follow the in vitro and in vivo distribution of nanocarriers and their payloads and the resulting biological effects.
the use of NIR fluorescence imaging in small animal models is a powerful method to study the fate of gene nanocarriers and to evaluate gene delivery efficiency.
NIR fluorescence imaging is the most promising technique to follow the fate of nanocarriers and the expression of genes and siRNAs, in vivo, in real time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NIR imaging of nucleic-acid nanocarriers is a powerful tool to study their pharmacokinetics in vivo.
NIR fluorescence imaging is a valuable tool to follow the biodistribution and the fate of nucleic acid-based nanocarriers and to evaluate the efficiency of gene and siRNA silencing in vivo.
NIR fluorescence imaging is a powerful tool for the investigation of nucleic acid delivery in vivo.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of NIR fluorescence imaging and bioluminescence imaging can provide a powerful tool for noninvasive in vivo monitoring of gene delivery and expression.
the use of NIR fluorophores is a promising tool for the development of new imaging probes and contrast agents, and for their use in preclinical studies.

NIR fluorescence and bioluminescence can be used to follow in vivo the biodistribution of nucleic acid nanostructures and their payload, to detect the expression of a reporter gene, to follow the release and biodistribution of a therapeutic nucleic acid, and to monitor the therapeutic effects.
